4.4. Demagnetizationresults
4.4.1. SillsassociatedwiththewesternlimboftheRLS
Sills BRC and RUD were generally characterized by magnetic re-
manentdirectionsthatdonotshowconsistencyatsitelevel.Apartfrom
these sites that will not be further discussed, demagnetization of the
remainingofsitesassociatedwiththewesternlimboftheRLSprovedto
be more successful. Samples were generally characterized by a max-
Fig.9.Cl-XMgdiagramforamphibolesandbiotitesfromsampleHWTshowing
imum of three magnetic components of geological significance.
theevolutionoftheirchemicalcompositionduringalteration.

showninFig.11.Summaryoftheremanentcomponentsidentifiedare
presentedinFig.12andlistedinTable7.

DuringAFandlowerheatingsteps(upto400°C–500°Cmaximum),
apresent-dayfield(PF)andtwoothermagneticcomponents(LT1and
LT2 respectively) were identified. The PF component was present in
sites BRA and RUI (Figs. 11 and 12) and removed during the pre-
treatmentorbythefirstheatingat100°C.
TheLT1componentwasidentifiedinsitesBRDandRUJasthefirst
componenttodemagnetize(Fig.11)whileitwasresolvedinsiteBRA
after the removalofthe PFcomponent. LT1 unblocking temperatures
are broadly distributed and this may be due tothe alteration state of
samples. In site BRD, this component consists of southerly and shal-
lowly inclined directions (LT1 + ) which were resolved at
250 °C–350 °C (Fig. 11). In sill BRA, the LT1 + component ex-
ceptionally persisted up to 530 °C-560 °C and constitutes the most
stablemagnetizationofthissite.InsiteRUJ,directionswithopposite
polarity (and thus labelled LT1-) were unblocked at temperatures
100°C-200°C(Figs.11and12)Table8.
TheLT2componentisorientedsoutherlywithanegativeinclination
andwasmanifestedinsitesBREduringtheAFpretreatment(Figs.11
and12).Duringthesame levelofdemagnetization,sillRUCrevealed
inconsistentdirections,afterwhichtheLT2componentwasseenupto
~350°C.TheLT2componentwasresolvedatmuchhighertemperature
(~500 °C or sometimes above) in site RUJ after the removal of the
magnetizationLT1–(Figs.11and12).
Upon removal of PF, LT1+/- and LT2 magnetic components, a
magnetization oriented northerly with a positive inclination (labelled
HIG+)wasidentifiedasstableendpointofdemagnetizationororigin-
seeking trajectories away from secondary components (Figs. 11 and
12).InsillRUF,whichisnotwell-preservedfromalteration,HIG+was
identifiedasthemoststablecomponent,butsamplesofthissitewere
fully demagnetized before 500 °C. In the other sites, the HIG+ com-
ponent was only resolved at higher temperatures (above 500 °C).
Maximumunblockingtemperaturesare575°C-580°C.
TheHIG+componentwasnotseeninsitesRUCandBRE.Instead,
these two sites recorded a characteristic magnetization oriented
southerlywithanegativeinclination(Fig.12).Thelattermagnetization
isreminiscenttotheLT2component,butisclearlyofhighercoercivity
(maximumunblockingtemperatureis~565°C),andthuslabelledHIG-.
TheunblockingtemperaturesoftheHIG+/-componentareconsistent
withtheideathatthisremanentmagnetizationiscarriedbyimpure(Ti-
bearing)magnetite.
4.4.2. BushveldsillsassociatedwiththeeasternlimboftheRLS
Behavior of samples from sills associated with the eastern limb of
theRLSduringstepwisedemagnetizationwasverycomparabletothat
ofsillsfromthewesternlimboftheRLS.Examplesofdemagnetization
behaviorsofindividualsamplesareshowninFig.13.Summaryofthe
remanentcomponentsidentifiedarepresentedinFig.14andlistedin
Table7.
DuringAFandlowerheatingsteps(upto450°C–500°Cgenerally),
severalmagneticcomponentscouldbeidentified.Infewsamples,these
componentssometimespersistedabovethetemperature500°C.
One poorly resolved low-coercivity component was seen in sites
HWU and HWW as the first component to demagnetize and was re-
movedbyheatingatabout350°C(Fig.13)andbefore(i.e.by100°C)
respectively. This component is essentially indistinguishable from the
PFcomponentpreviouslyseeninsillsassociatedtothewesternlimbof
theRLS(compareFigs.12and14).
Another low-coercivity magnetic direction was identified in site
HWXattemperatureof350°Corsometimeshigher(upto500°C)as
shallowlyinclinedandsoutherlyorienteddirections(Fig.14)similarto
thepreviouslydescribedcomponentLT1+(seeFig.12).InsiteHWV,
another shallow component but more westerly oriented was removed
byheatingtotemperatures100–200°C(Figs.13and14).
Thelastlow-coercivitycomponentisreminiscenttothepreviously
describedLT2componentasitconsistsofeasterlytosoutheasterlyor-
ienteddirectionswithpositiveinclinations(compareFigs.12and14).

4.5.1. Secondarymagnetizations(LT1+/-andLT2)
The LT1+/- magnetization (Fig. 15) bears some resemblance to
dual-polarityUmkondomagneticdirections(e.g.Swanson-Hyselletal.,
2015) and was thus probably recorded during the Umkondo igneous
eventat~1.1Ga.
The LT2 remanence (Fig. 15) generally shares similarities with
primary magnetic directions reported from various 1.9 Ga−1.8 Ga-
agedrockunitsoftheKaapvaalCraton(e.g.DeKocketal.,2006;Letts
et al., 2005, Wabo et al., 2019) and is thus interpreted as a thermal
disturbancelinkedtotheseigneousevents.
4.5.2. HIG+/-characteristicmagnetization
TheHIG+/-characteristicremanence(Fig.16a)isthemostprolific
magnetization of the sampling sills. Site means with a semi-angle of
95%coneofconfidence(α95)higherthan 18°arediscardedfromthe
discussion.Intheremainingsites,theHIG-andHIG+directionsare
notstrictlyantipodalandthereversaltest(McFaddenandMcElhinny
1990)revealsthattheangle(γo=21.23°)betweenthesetwomeansis
higherthanthecriticalangle(γc=9.67°)requiredforapositiveresult.
However, the test must be considered inconclusive, given the limited
numberofsitesthatrecordedthenegativepolarity.
The exact timing of acquisition of the HIG+/- magnetization re-
mains uncertain given the absence of field tests for paleomagnetic
stability. However, we tentatively interpret this magnetization to be
primarybasedonseveralreasons.Firstly,theHIG+/-componentsthat
constitute the characteristic (i.e. thermoremanent) magnetizations of
samplesarecarriedbyTi-magnetiteswithahighunblockingtempera-
ture of 560 °C–575 °C. A mixture with thermo-chemical or chemical
overprints would require that the Ti-magnetites actually include a
primaryandsecondarymineralgenerations,allwithverysimilargrain
sizeasindicatedbysimilarunblockingtemperatures.Thisrequirement
seems unlikely for samples collected regionally from small size intru-
sions with simpler (quick) cooling histories (e.g. Snelling, 1991) and
that have been showed to be largely preserved from alteration. Sec-
ondly, the HIG+/- site means do not plot identical like it would be
expectedinthecase ofpervasiveremagnetization (e.g.Butler, 1992).
Instead,theyshowsomedegreeofscatter(Fig.16a),suggestingaseries
of spot readings recorded by individual sill during intrusion and sub-
sequentcoolinginashortperiodoftimerelativetosecularvariationof
the Earth's magnetic field. This argument, albeit somewhat circum-
stantial,hasbeenusedbypreviousauthors(e.g.BatesandJones,1996;
McEnroe and Brown, 2000) to support the primary nature of magne-
tization in rocks in the absence of field tests. Here, the record of pa-
leosecularvariationisconsistentwithcompositionalvariationsofsills
which indicate some degree of differentiation and thus time gap be-
tweensillcrystallization.Lastly,theHIG+/-sitemeansgroupbetterin
stratigraphic than in geographic coordinates, (clustering parameter k
increasesfrom22.90to40.10uponapplicationofthetectoniccorrec-
Fig.10.40Ar/39AragespectraandcorrespondingCl/Kratiosofbiotite(aand tion;seeTable7).However,giventhelittlevariationintheorientation
b) and 40Ar/ 39Ar age spectrum of amphibole (c) from sample HWT. ofthestratasampledinthisstudy,thebootstrapfoldtest(Tauxeetal.,
